Al-Khiḍr, companion of Moses ﵇. Authorities disagree over his lineage, whether he was a prophet, the length of his life, and whether he remained alive. If he survived until the time of the Prophet ﷺ and remained alive thereafter, he falls within one definition of a Companion. I have not found any of the early authorities who listed him among the Companions, although most accepted the reports concerning his longevity and survival. I have collected the reports about him that came to my knowledge, explaining which are sound and which are not.

Lineage

It is said that he was a direct son of Adam. Al-Dāraquṭnī transmitted this view in al-Afrād by way of Rawwād ibn al-Jarrāḥ, from Muqātil ibn Sulaymān, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās. Rawwād is weak, Muqātil is abandoned, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk did not hear from Ibn ʿAbbās. The second view is that he was a son of Cain son of Adam. Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī mentioned this in Kitāb al-Muʿammarīn, saying: ‘Our shaykhs, including Abū ʿUbayda, related it and said that he was the longest-lived of humankind.’ This chain is missing successive links. The proponent of this view related that his name was Khiḍrūn, namely al-Khiḍr. It is also said that his name was ʿĀmir; Abū al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Diḥya reported that from Ibn Ḥabīb al-Baghdādī.

The third view comes from Wahb ibn Munabbih: that he was Balyā ibn Malkān ibn Fāligh ibn Shālikh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Noah. Ibn Qutayba held this view, and al-Nawawī related it, adding that Kalmān is also reported in place of Malkān. The fourth view comes from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Uways: that he was al-Muʿammar ibn Mālik ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Naṣr ibn al-Azd. The fifth view is that he was the son of ʿAmāʾīl ibn al-Nawwār ibn al-ʿĪṣ ibn Isaac. Ibn Qutayba also related this, and Muqātil likewise named his father ʿAmāʾīl. The sixth view is that he belonged to the tribe of Aaron, brother of Moses. It is narrated from al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayra, from Ibn ʿAbbās, but it is remote. Even more surprising is Ibn Isḥāq’s statement that he was Armā ibn Khalafyā, which Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr rejected. The seventh view is that he was a daughter’s son of Pharaoh; Muḥammad ibn Ayyūb related it from Ibn Lahīʿa. It is also said that he was a direct son of Pharaoh, as al-Naqqāsh related. The eighth view is that he was Elisha, also related from Muqātil, and it too is remote. The ninth view is that he descended from Qāris. This comes from Ibn Shawdhab; al-Ṭabarī transmitted it with a good chain from Ḍamra ibn Rabīʿa, from Ibn Shawdhab. The tenth view is that he descended from one of those who believed in Abraham and emigrated with him from Babylonia. Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī related this in his Tārīkh. It is also said that his father was Persian and his mother Roman, and conversely that his father was Roman and his mother Persian.

It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections that he was called al-Khiḍr because he sat upon a white furwa and it began turning green beneath him. This is Aḥmad’s wording, narrated by Ibn al-Mubārak from Maʿmar, from Hammām, from Abū Hurayra. Furwa here means dry ground. Aḥmad said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; Maʿmar informed us, from Hammām, from Abū Hurayra, who elevated it: ‘He was called al-Khiḍr only because he sat upon a furwa and it stirred green beneath him.’ Furwa here means pale grass. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad said: ‘I think this explanation is ʿAbd al-Razzāq’s.’ Reports on the subject also come from Ibn ʿAbbās, by way of Qatāda from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith, and by way of Manṣūr from Mujāhid. Al-Nawawī said that his teknonym was Abū al-ʿAbbās, and this is agreed upon.

What Has Been Reported About His Being a Prophet

God Most High relates his statement in the account with Moses: ‘I did not do it on my own command’ [Qur’an 18:82]. Its apparent meaning is that he acted at God’s command, and the presumption is that there was no intermediary. It is possible that the command came through another unnamed prophet, but that is remote. It cannot be said that this was mere inspiration, for inspiration to someone who is not a prophet does not constitute revelation that authorizes killing a person or exposing people to drowning. If we hold that he was a prophet, there is no difficulty. Moreover, how could someone who was not a prophet possess knowledge surpassing a prophet’s? The Prophet ﷺ stated in the sound report that God told Moses, ‘Indeed, Our servant Khiḍr.’ How, moreover, could a prophet follow someone who was not a prophet? Al-Thaʿlabī said that al-Khiḍr was a prophet under every view. One of the leading scholars used to say: ‘The first knot of heresy to be undone is belief that al-Khiḍr was a prophet,’ because heretics exploit the claim that he was not a prophet to assert that a saint is superior to a prophet, as one of them said:

The station of prophecy lies in an isthmus,
just above the messenger and below the saint.

Those who held that he was a prophet then disagreed over whether he was a messenger. Ibn ʿAbbās and Wahb ibn Munabbih held that he was a prophet but not a messenger. Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ziyād, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, and some People of the Book held that he was sent to his people and that they responded to him. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Rummānī, followed by Ibn al-Jawzī, supported this view. Al-Thaʿlabī said: ‘Under every view he is a prophet, long-lived and concealed from sight.’ Abū Ḥayyān said in his Tafsīr: ‘The majority hold that he was a prophet. His knowledge concerned inward realities revealed to him, while Moses’ knowledge concerned judgment by outward appearances.’ A group of Sufis held that he was a saint. This was also the view of Abū ʿAlī ibn Abī Mūsā among the Ḥanbalīs and Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī in al-Zāhir, after the latter related the scholars’ two views as to whether he was a prophet or a saint. Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī said in his Risāla: ‘Al-Khiḍr was not a prophet, but a saint.’ Al-Māwardī related a third view: that he was an angel who assumed human form. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Diḥya said: ‘We do not know whether he was an angel, a prophet, or a righteous servant.’

By way of Abū Ṣāliḥ, al-Layth’s scribe, from Yaḥyā ibn Ayyūb, from Khālid ibn Yazīd, it is reported that Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: ‘Al-Khiḍr ibn ʿĀmīl embarked with a group of his companions until he reached the Indian Ocean, namely the Sea of China. He said, “My companions, lower me.” They lowered him into the sea for days and nights, after which he ascended. They asked, “Khiḍr, what did you see? God has honored you and preserved your life in the depths of this sea.” He replied, “An angel met me and said, ‘Erring human, where are you going and where have you come from?’ I said, ‘I wished to see the depth of this sea.’ He replied, ‘How can you, when a man has been falling through it since the time of the Prophet David ﵇ and has not yet reached a third of its depth, although three hundred years have passed?’”’ Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it in Kaʿb’s biography in al-Ḥilya.

Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr said in his Tārīkh that according to the generality of the earliest People of the Book, al-Khiḍr lived in the days of King Afrīdūn. It is also said that he commanded the vanguard of the elder Dhū al-Qarnayn who lived in the days of Abraham. With that Dhū al-Qarnayn, whose vanguard he commanded, he reached the River of Life and unknowingly drank its water, while Dhū al-Qarnayn and his companions did not know. He thus became immortal and, according to them, remains alive to this day. Ibn Jarīr said that Ibn Isḥāq mentioned that God placed a man of the Israelites in authority over them and sent al-Khiḍr as a prophet with him. Ibn Jarīr said: ‘More than a thousand years separate this time from Afrīdūn. The view that he lived in Afrīdūn’s days is more plausible, unless the statement means that he was not sent as a prophet until the time of that king.’ I say: the words ‘He sent al-Khiḍr as a prophet with him’ may instead mean that God supported the man with al-Khiḍr. Unless that was the moment al-Khiḍr’s prophethood began, there is nothing to prevent his having been a prophet beforehand and then being sent with that king. I say this because most of his reports with Moses are evidence supporting the view that he was a prophet.

A group of authorities mentioned his story with Dhū al-Qarnayn, including Khaythama ibn Sulaymān by way of Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, from his father: Dhū al-Qarnayn had an angel as a friend and asked him to direct him to something that would lengthen his life. The angel directed him to the Spring of Life within the darkness. He traveled to it with al-Khiḍr in his vanguard, and al-Khiḍr reached it while Dhū al-Qarnayn did not. Another proof cited for his prophethood is what ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted, by way of al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, who said: when Moses met al-Khiḍr, he said, ‘Peace be upon you, Khiḍr.’ Al-Khiḍr replied, ‘And upon you be peace, Moses.’ Moses asked, ‘How do you know that I am Moses?’ He replied, ‘The One who made you know me made me know you.’ Wahb ibn Munabbih said in al-Mubtadaʾ that God Most High said to al-Khiḍr: ‘I loved you before I created you; I sanctified you when I created you; and I loved you after I created you.’ He was a prophet sent to the Israelites to renew the covenant of Moses. When grave events multiplied among the Israelites and Nebuchadnezzar was given power over them, al-Khiḍr wandered the earth with the wild animals, and God deferred his term for as long as He willed. He is the one whom people see.

Reports Concerning His Longevity and Its Cause

Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated with the preceding chain from Ibn ʿAbbās that al-Khiḍr’s term was deferred until the Antichrist should be exposed as a liar. Ibn Isḥāq said in al-Mubtadaʾ that when death approached Adam, he gathered his descendants and said that God Most High would send a punishment upon the people of the earth, so they should keep his body with them in the cave until they could bury him in Syria. When the Flood came, Noah told his descendants that Adam had prayed to God to prolong the life of the person who buried him until the Day of Resurrection. Adam’s body remained until al-Khiḍr undertook his burial, whereupon God fulfilled for him what He had promised and he remained alive for as long as God willed. Abū Mikhnaf Lūṭ ibn Yaḥyā said at the beginning of his Kitāb al-Muʿammarīn that the scholars who knew and collected reports unanimously held al-Khiḍr to be the longest-lived human being, and that he was Khiḍrūn ibn Cain ibn Adam.

In Dhū al-Qarnayn’s biography, Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted through Khaythama ibn Sulaymān, from Abū ʿUbayda ibn the nephew of Hannād, from Sufyān ibn Wakīʿ, from his father, from Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān, from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, who was asked about Dhū al-Qarnayn. He said that Dhū al-Qarnayn was a righteous servant of God, held in a lofty station by Him, who ruled everything between east and west. He had an angelic friend named Raphael who visited him. As they conversed, Dhū al-Qarnayn asked him about worship in heaven. Raphael wept and said: ‘What is your worship beside ours? In heaven are angels who stand and never sit, prostrate and never rise, and bow and never stand erect. They say, “Our Lord, we have not worshipped You as You deserve.”’ Dhū al-Qarnayn wept and said that he wished to live long enough to worship his Lord in full obedience. Raphael told him of God’s Spring of Life: anyone who drank once from it would never die until he himself asked his Lord for death. Its location was unknown, though the angels spoke of a darkness on earth never trodden by human or jinn and supposed the spring to be there.

Dhū al-Qarnayn gathered the earth’s scholars. They did not know the Spring of Life, but one scholar had read in Adam’s testament of the darkness at the horn of the sun. Dhū al-Qarnayn prepared and traveled for twelve years until he reached it. It was not night but surged like smoke. When his armies tried to dissuade him, and the scholars warned him lest God become angry with them, he refused. He chose six thousand men upon six thousand virgin mares, appointed al-Khiḍr over a vanguard of two thousand, and entered. Al-Khiḍr knew what he sought, though Dhū al-Qarnayn concealed it. A valley crossed al-Khiḍr’s path, and he supposed the spring might be there. He halted his companions, went on alone, and found a spring whose water was whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. He drank, performed ablution, and bathed, then dressed and left. Dhū al-Qarnayn passed by but missed it in the darkness. The rest of the report follows.

It is related from Sulaymān al-Ashajj, a companion of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, from Kaʿb that al-Khiḍr was Dhū al-Qarnayn’s vizier. Standing with him upon an Indian mountain, he saw a leaf bearing: ‘In the name of God, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. From Adam, father of humankind, to his descendants: I counsel you to fear God and warn you against the stratagem of my enemy and yours, Iblīs, for he caused me to be sent down here.’ Dhū al-Qarnayn descended and measured the place where Adam had sat; it was one hundred and thirty miles. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said that Elias was assigned to the deserts and al-Khiḍr to the seas; both were granted immortality in this world until the first Blast, and they meet every pilgrimage season.

Al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Usāma narrated in his Musnad from ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ibn Wāqid, from Muḥammad ibn Bahrām, from Abān, from Anas that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘Al-Khiḍr is in the sea and Elisha is on land. They meet each night at the barrier Dhū al-Qarnayn built between humankind and Gog and Magog. Each year they perform Hajj and ʿumra and drink one draught from your Zamzam that suffices them until the next year.’ I say: ʿAbd al-Raḥīm and Abān are both abandoned. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīra related from Thawr, from Khālid ibn Maʿdān, from Kaʿb that al-Khiḍr sits upon a pulpit of light between the upper and lower sea; the creatures of the sea have been commanded to hear and obey him, and spirits are presented to him morning and evening. Al-ʿUqaylī cited it and said that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīra relates reports without foundation; Ibn Yūnus called him objectionable in hadith.

Ibn Shāhīn transmitted with a weak chain to Khuṣayf that four prophets are alive: Jesus and Enoch in heaven, and al-Khiḍr and Elias on earth—al-Khiḍr at sea and his companion on land. Many reports of this sort will appear in the final chapter. Al-Thaʿlabī said that al-Khiḍr is said not to die until the end of time, when the Qur’an is taken away. Al-Nawawī said in his Tahdhīb that most scholars held him alive and present among us; among Sufis and people of righteousness and spiritual knowledge this was agreed, and their accounts of seeing, meeting, learning from, questioning, and receiving answers from him at noble and virtuous places were too numerous to count and too famous to mention. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ said in his Fatāwā that the great majority of righteous scholars and ordinary people held him alive, and only some hadith scholars departed from them by denying it.

I say: some later writers carefully collected stories transmitted from righteous persons and others after the year 320, even though some chains contain men weakened for frequent errors or accused of lying, such as Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Jahḍam. One cannot argue that these stories establish mass transmission in meaning merely because the reliability and probity of each transmitter is not required for mass transmission. The essential condition is that the report come through a number whose collusion upon a lie is ordinarily impossible. If their wording agrees, that is literal mass transmission; if it differs, whatever all share is mass transmission in meaning. These stories share the claim that al-Khiḍr is alive, but one version that definitively explains his survival holds that every age has its own ‘Khiḍr’: he is the chief of the saints, and whenever one chief dies, another is installed in his place and called al-Khiḍr. A group of Sufis circulated this position without objection among themselves. On that account, one cannot be certain that everyone described as al-Khiḍr was Moses’ companion; he may instead have been the Khiḍr of that age. Their conflicting descriptions support this: some saw an old man, others a mature man, and others a young man, which may be understood as different persons seen at different times. والله أعلم

Al-Suhaylī said in al-Taʿrīf wa-l-Aʿlām that al-Khiḍr’s name was disputed. After mentioning some of the foregoing views, he related the claim that he was the son of ʿĀmīl ibn Samāṭīn—Armā ibn Khalafā ibn Esau ibn Isaac—and that his father was a king and his mother a Persian woman named Ilhā. She bore him in a cave, where a ewe from a villager’s flock was found nursing him each day. The villager took him and raised him. When he grew up, the king sought a scribe to copy the scriptures revealed to Abraham and gathered people of learning and distinction. Among those brought before him was his son al-Khiḍr, whom he did not recognize. Impressed by his handwriting and knowledge, the king investigated until he learned that he was his son, embraced him, and placed him over the people. Al-Khiḍr later fled from the king for reasons too lengthy to recount, found the Spring of Life, and drank from it. He remains alive until the Antichrist emerges; he is the man whom the Antichrist kills and then revives.

Al-Suhaylī said: ‘It is claimed that he did not reach the time of the Prophet ﷺ, but this is unsound.’ He also said that al-Bukhārī and a group of hadith scholars held that al-Khiḍr died before one hundred years after the Hijra had elapsed. Their teacher Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī championed that view on account of the Prophet ﷺ saying, ‘At the turn of one hundred years, no one now upon the earth will remain’—meaning those who were alive when he said it. As for al-Khiḍr’s meeting the Prophet ﷺ and consoling the Prophet’s family while they had gathered to wash him ﷺ, al-Suhaylī cited a report in which the Companions, while being consoled over the Prophet ﷺ, heard words but did not see the speaker, and ʿAlī told them, ‘That is al-Khiḍr.’ He added that Ibn Abī al-Dunyā transmitted through Makḥūl, from Anas, a meeting between the prophet Elias and the Prophet ﷺ, and reasoned that if Elias could remain until the Prophetic era, al-Khiḍr could likewise remain. This is the substance of his words.

Abū al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Diḥya objected that none of the routes al-Suhaylī indicated was sound and that al-Khiḍr’s meeting with any prophet except Moses was unestablished, as God related in his account. By agreement of the hadith authorities, nothing transmitted concerning his continued life is sound. Those who report such material omit its defect either because they do not know it or because it is obvious to hadith scholars. Stories from shaykhs are themselves objectionable: how can a rational person meet someone unknown, hear him say ‘I am so-and-so,’ and believe him? The consolation report Abū ʿUmar cited is fabricated; ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muḥarrar, an abandoned transmitter, related it from Yazīd ibn al-Aṣamm, from ʿAlī. As Muslim records in the introduction to his Ṣaḥīḥ, Ibn al-Mubārak said of Ibn Muḥarrar: ‘When I saw him, a piece of dung was dearer to me than he was’—preferring the sight of filth to seeing him. I say: the consolation is reported by a route other than ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muḥarrar, as I shall mention below. The report of Makḥūl from Anas is fabricated; Ibn Diḥya then transmitted its rejection from Aḥmad, Yaḥyā, Isḥāq, and Abū Zurʿa. Its text is manifestly objectionable and belongs to fables. This is the substance of his words. I shall cite the Anas report in full and show that it has a route other than the one al-Suhaylī indicated.

Those who held al-Khiḍr long-lived relied upon the story of the Spring of Life and upon its mention in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, but none of that is established as a statement elevated to the Prophet ﷺ, so the matter must be critically examined.

Reports About Al-Khiḍr Before the Prophet’s Mission

God Most High has related in His Book what happened to Moses ﵇. The two shaykhs transmitted it by several routes from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. Other versions contain additions absent from the Ṣaḥīḥ, all of which I have treated in Fatḥ al-Bārī. It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections that the Prophet ﷺ said: ‘I wish Moses had been patient, so that more of their affair would have been related to us.’ One who claimed that al-Khiḍr was no longer living when this was said argued from it that, had he been alive, one of the senior Companions could have accompanied him and witnessed something like what Moses saw. Those who claim his survival reply that the wish concerned what would have occurred specifically between him and Moses ﵇, and that no one else could take Moses’ place.

Among reports of al-Khiḍr with someone other than Moses is one transmitted by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr through two routes from Baqiyya ibn al-Walīd, from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād al-Alhānī, from Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī: the Messenger of God ﷺ asked his Companions, ‘Shall I tell you about al-Khiḍr?’ They said, ‘Yes, Messenger of God.’ He said: ‘One day, while al-Khiḍr walked through a market of the Israelites, a slave under a manumission contract saw him and said, “Give me charity; may God bless you.” Al-Khiḍr replied, “I believe in God. Whatever God wills comes to pass. I have nothing to give you.” The poor man said, “I ask you by the Face of God to give me charity, for I see generosity in your face and hope for blessing from you.” Al-Khiḍr said, “I believe in God. I have nothing to give unless you take me and sell me.” The poor man asked, “Can that be right?” He said, “Yes. I speak the truth. You have asked me by a tremendous thing, and I will not disappoint you when asked by the Face of my Lord.”’

The poor man took him to the market and sold him for four hundred dirhams. He remained with the buyer for a time without being put to any task, then said: ‘You bought me seeking some good from me, so command me to work.’ The man replied: ‘I dislike burdening you; you are an old, weak man.’ Al-Khiḍr said it would not burden him, so the man told him to move some stones that no fewer than six men could move in a day. The man then left on an errand.

When he returned, al-Khiḍr had moved the stones in an hour. The man said: ‘You have done well and graciously, and proved capable of what I did not think you could do.’ The man then had to travel and said: ‘I believe you trustworthy, so look after my household well while I am away.’ Al-Khiḍr agreed and asked for a task. Again the man disliked burdening him, but al-Khiḍr insisted it would not be a burden. The man told him to make mud bricks for his house before he returned. When the man came back from his journey, al-Khiḍr had erected the building. He said: ‘I ask you by the Face of God: what is your story and what is your affair?’ Al-Khiḍr replied: ‘You have asked me by the Face of God, and it was the Face of God that placed me in slavery. I shall tell you who I am. I am the al-Khiḍr of whom you have heard. A poor man asked me for charity, and I had nothing to give. He asked me by the Face of God, so I surrendered my person to him and he sold me. I tell you that whoever is asked by the Face of God and turns the petitioner away despite being able to give will stand on the Day of Resurrection with neither skin, flesh, nor bone upon his face—nothing but a rattling frame.”’

The man said: ‘I believe in God. Prophet of God, I burdened you without knowing.’ Al-Khiḍr replied: ‘No harm; you acted well and preserved my welfare.’ The man said: ‘May my father and mother be your ransom, Prophet of God. Dispose of my family and property as you wish, or choose and I shall set you free.’ Al-Khiḍr said: ‘I would like you to free me so I may worship my Lord.’ The man freed him, and al-Khiḍr said: ‘Praise be to God, who bound me in slavery and then delivered me from it.’ I say: this hadith’s chain would be fair were it not for Baqiyya’s ambiguous transmission. If established, it would be explicit proof that al-Khiḍr was a prophet, for the Prophet ﷺ related the man’s address, ‘Prophet of God,’ and tacitly approved it.

Those Who Held That Al-Khiḍr Had Died

Abū Bakr al-Naqqāsh transmitted in his Tafsīr from ʿAlī ibn Mūsā al-Riḍā and from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Bukhārī that al-Khiḍr had died. When al-Bukhārī was asked whether he was alive, he rejected the claim and cited the hadith that at the turn of one hundred years none then upon the face of the earth would remain. He himself transmitted this report in the Ṣaḥīḥ from Ibn ʿUmar, and it is the principal proof of those who held that al-Khiḍr died and denied that he remained alive. Abū Ḥayyān said in his Tafsīr that the majority held he had died. He transmitted from Ibn Abī al-Faḍl al-Mursī that al-Khiḍr, Moses’ companion, had died, because had he been alive he would have had to come to the Prophet ﷺ, believe in him, and follow him. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: ‘Were Moses alive, he would have no choice but to follow me.’ Al-Mursī suggested that the al-Khiḍr now claimed was someone other than Moses’ companion. Others claimed every age has a Khiḍr, but that assertion has no proof.

In his book devoted to al-Khiḍr’s biography, Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī transmitted from Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī that al-Khiḍr had died, and Ibn al-Munādī himself stated that conclusion categorically. He also transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Mūsā al-Riḍā, from Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from his father: near the end of his life, the Messenger of God ﷺ once led the night prayer. After concluding it, he said: ‘Consider this night of yours: at the turn of one hundred years, no one upon the face of the earth will remain.’ Muslim transmitted from Jābir that the Messenger of God ﷺ said a month before his death: ‘You ask me about the Hour, but knowledge of it rests only with God. By God, no living soul upon the earth will survive one hundred years.’ This is Abū al-Zubayr’s version from Jābir. In Abū Naḍra’s version, he said shortly before his death, or one month before it, ‘No living soul,’ and added at the end, ‘that was then alive.’ Al-Tirmidhī transmitted from Abū Sufyān, from Jābir, something like Abū al-Zubayr’s version.

In his treatise on the question, Ibn al-Jawzī reported that Abū Yaʿlā ibn al-Farrāʾ al-Ḥanbalī said one of their colleagues was asked whether al-Khiḍr had died and answered yes. Abū Yaʿlā had heard the same from Abū Ṭāhir ibn al-ʿAbbādī, who argued that had al-Khiḍr been alive he would have come to the Prophet ﷺ. I say: those holding this view also include Abū al-Faḍl ibn Nāṣir, Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī, and Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Naqqāsh.

Ibn al-Jawzī argued that if al-Khiḍr had remained alive since Moses’ time or earlier, the size of his body would have corresponded to the bodies of those ancient people. He then transmitted through his chain from Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī that Daniel’s nose was one cubit long. When Daniel’s body was uncovered in Abū Mūsā’s time, a man stood beside him and Daniel’s knee was level with the man’s head. Yet nothing in all the stories of those who claim to have seen al-Khiḍr suggests that his body differed from theirs. Ibn al-Jawzī also cited Aḥmad’s report by way of Mujāhid, from al-Shaʿbī, from Jābir, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, were Moses alive, he would have no choice but to follow me.’ If that applies to Moses, how could al-Khiḍr, if alive, fail to follow him, pray the Friday and congregational prayers with him, and strive under his banner—just as it is established that Jesus will pray behind an imam of this community?

He further cited God Most High’s words, ‘And when God took the covenant of the prophets’ [Qur’an 3:81]. Ibn ʿAbbās said that whenever God sent a prophet, He took from him the covenant that if Muḥammad were sent while he was alive, he would believe in him and support him. Had al-Khiḍr existed during the Prophet’s time ﷺ, he would have come to him, supported him with hand and tongue, and fought beneath his banner. That would also have been among the greatest causes for most of the People of the Book—who knew the story of al-Khiḍr and Moses—to believe.

Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī said: ‘I investigated al-Khiḍr’s alleged longevity and whether he remained alive. Most heedless people are deceived into believing he remains because of what is related about it. The elevated hadiths on the subject are feeble, and chains through the People of the Book are fallen because they cannot be trusted. The story of Maslama ibn Maṣqala is like a fable, and the report of Riyāḥ is like the wind. All the other reports are weak from beginning to end. Either they were foisted upon trustworthy transmitters while those transmitters were inattentive, or some narrator deliberately fabricated them. God Most High has said, “We did not grant immortality to any human before you” [Qur’an 21:34]. Hadith scholars say that the Anas report has an objectionable chain and a sick text, and that al-Khiḍr neither corresponded with nor met any prophet. Had al-Khiḍr been alive, he could not have failed to join the Messenger of God ﷺ and emigrate to him.’

Ibn al-Munādī added that one of his colleagues told him Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī was asked about al-Khiḍr’s longevity and denied it, saying that he had died long ago. Another scholar, asked again about his longevity, replied: ‘No one can obtain justice from someone who refers the matter to an absent living man or a missing dead man. Only Satan cast this idea among the people.’ This is the end of his statement. I have cited the reports to which he alluded and added many other things of their kind. The route of nearly every one contains a defect. God is the One whose aid is sought.

Al-Aṣbahānī’s Tafsīr relates that al-Ḥasan held al-Khiḍr to have died. It also reports that when al-Bukhārī was asked whether al-Khiḍr and Elias were among the living, he answered: ‘How can that be, when the Prophet ﷺ said near the end of his life, “Consider this night of yours: at the turn of one hundred years, no one now upon the face of the earth will remain”?’ Ibn al-Jawzī also cited the established report in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī that on the day of Badr the Prophet ﷺ said: ‘O God, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped upon the earth.’ Al-Khiḍr was not among them; had he been alive that day, he would have fallen within this general statement, since he certainly worshipped God.

Another scholar cited the Prophet’s words ﷺ, ‘There is no prophet after me,’ and ascribed this argument to Ibn Diḥya. The argument is countered by Jesus son of Mary, who is certainly a prophet and who, as established, will descend to earth at the end of time and judge by the law of the Prophet ﷺ. The negation must therefore mean that no new person will be made a prophet, not that no prophet commissioned before then can continue to exist.

Reports Claiming That Al-Khiḍr Lived in the Time of the Prophet ﷺ and From Then Until the Present

Ibn ʿAdī transmitted in al-Kāmil by way of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nāfiʿ, from Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, from his father, from his grandfather, that while the Messenger of God ﷺ was in the mosque he heard speech behind him. A man was saying, ‘O God, help me to attain what will save me from that of which You have made me afraid.’ On hearing it, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘Why do you not add its sister?’ The man then said: ‘O God, grant me the longing of the righteous for that toward which You have made them long.’ The Prophet ﷺ told Anas ibn Mālik: ‘Go to him, Anas, and tell him that the Messenger of God ﷺ asks him to seek forgiveness for me.’ When Anas conveyed that, the man asked whether he was the Messenger’s envoy and told him to return and verify it. The Prophet ﷺ said: ‘Tell him yes.’ The man then said: ‘Go and tell him: God has favored you above the prophets as He favored Ramadan above the months, and favored your community above the communities as He favored Friday above all other days.’ Anas went to look at him and found that he was al-Khiḍr. The leading critics weakened Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, but this report came through another route.

Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī said that Abū Jaʿfar Aḥmad ibn al-Naḍr al-ʿAskarī informed him that Muḥammad ibn Sallām al-Manbijī related it to them. Ibn ʿAsākir also transmitted, by way of Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl ibn Jābir, from Muḥammad ibn Sallām al-Manbijī, from Waḍḍāḥ ibn ʿAbbād al-Kūfī, from ʿĀṣim ibn Sulaymān al-Aḥwal, from Anas ibn Mālik. Anas said: ‘One night I went out carrying water for the Prophet ﷺ to perform purification. He heard a caller and told me, “Anas, be quiet.” I fell silent and he listened. The caller said, “O God, help me to attain what will save me from that of which You have made me afraid.” The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “If only he would say its sister with it.” It was as though the man was prompted to say what the Prophet ﷺ wanted, for he added, “And grant me the longing of the righteous for that toward which You have made them long.”

‘The Prophet ﷺ said: “Anas, set down the water and go to this caller. Tell him to pray that God assist the Messenger of God in the mission for which He sent him, and to pray that his community accept in truth what their Prophet has brought them.” I went to him and said: “May God have mercy on you. Pray that God assist the Messenger of God in the mission for which He sent him, and pray that his community accept in truth what their Prophet has brought them.” He asked who had sent me. I disliked telling him without having asked the Messenger of God’s permission ﷺ, so I replied: “May God have mercy on you, what harm is there in knowing who sent me? Pray for what I conveyed.” He refused unless I identified the sender. I returned to the Messenger of God ﷺ and told him. He said: “Go back and tell him I am the Messenger’s envoy.”

‘I returned and did so. He said: “Welcome to the envoy of the Messenger of God. I had more right to go to him. Convey my greeting of peace to the Messenger of God ﷺ.” He also said: “Messenger of God, al-Khiḍr greets you with peace and God’s mercy and tells you that God has favored you above the prophets as He favored Ramadan above all other months, and favored your community above the communities as He favored Friday above all other days.” As I turned away, I heard him say: “O God, make me one of this rightly guided community that receives mercy, repentance, and pardon.”’

Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it in al-Awsaṭ from Bishr ibn ʿAlī ibn Bishr al-ʿAmmī, from Muḥammad ibn Sallām, and said that none related it from Anas except ʿĀṣim, none from ʿĀṣim except Waḍḍāḥ, and Muḥammad ibn Sallām alone related it from Waḍḍāḥ. I say: it has come through two other routes from Anas. Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī said: ‘This hadith is feeble because of Waḍḍāḥ and others. Its chain is objectionable and its text sick. Al-Khiḍr neither corresponded with nor met our Prophet ﷺ.’ Ibn al-Jawzī considered it implausible that al-Khiḍr could meet the Prophet ﷺ and assemble with him, yet not come to him. Ibn ʿAsākir also transmitted by way of Abū Khālid, the muezzin of the mosque of Musaylima, from Abū Dāwūd, from Anas, a similar report.

Ibn Shāhīn said: Mūsā ibn Anas ibn Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ṭalḥa ibn Mūsā ibn Anas ibn Mālik related to us, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī, from Ḥātim ibn Abī Rawwād, from Muʿādh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr, from his father, from Anas. Anas said: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ went out one night on an errand, and I followed. We heard someone saying, “O God, I ask You for the longing of the truthful for that toward which You have made them long.” The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “What a prayer, if he would add its sister.” We then heard the speaker say: “O God, I ask You to help me attain what will save me from that of which You have made me afraid.” The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “It has been made certain, by the Lord of the Kaʿba. Anas, go to the man and ask him to pray that God grant His Messenger ﷺ acceptance from his community and assistance in what he brought of the truth and confirmation.”

‘I went to the man and said: “Servant of God, pray for the Messenger of God.” He asked who I was. I disliked telling him without permission, and he refused to pray until I did. I returned to the Messenger of God ﷺ and told him, and he instructed me to identify myself. I returned and said: “I am the envoy of the Messenger of God.” He replied: “Welcome to the Messenger of God and to the envoy of the Messenger of God. Pray for him, convey my greeting of peace, and tell him: ‘I am your brother al-Khiḍr, and I had more right to come to you.’” As I turned away, I heard him saying: “O God, make me one of this community that receives mercy and repentance.”’

Al-Dāraquṭnī said in al-Afrād that Aḥmad ibn al-ʿAbbās al-Baghawī related it from Anas ibn Khālid, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, similarly. This Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh is Abū Salama al-Anṣārī, whose hadith is extremely feeble. He is not al-Bukhārī’s shaykh, the judge of Basra; that man is trustworthy and earlier than Abū Salama.

In the Fawāʾid of Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad al-Muzakkī, as selected by al-Dāraquṭnī, we transmitted from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Khuzayma, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Zayd, from ʿAmr ibn ʿĀṣim, from al-Ḥasan ibn Razīn, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who—I do not know otherwise—elevated it to the Prophet ﷺ: ‘Al-Khiḍr and Elias meet every year during the pilgrimage season. Each shaves the other’s head, and they part after reciting these words: “In the name of God; what God wills. Nothing brings good but God. In the name of God; what God wills. Nothing averts evil but God. In the name of God; what God wills. Whatever blessing there is comes from God. In the name of God; what God wills. There is no power or strength except through God.”’ Al-Dāraquṭnī said in al-Afrād that no one except al-Ḥasan ibn Razīn related it from Ibn Jurayj. Abū Jaʿfar al-ʿUqaylī said that he was not corroborated, was unknown, and his hadith was not preserved. Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī called the hadith feeble because of al-Ḥasan.

It also came by another route, but an extremely feeble one. Ibn al-Jawzī transmitted by way of Aḥmad ibn ʿAmmār, from Muḥammad ibn Mahdī, from Mahdī ibn Hilāl, from Ibn Jurayj: ‘The two who inhabit land and sea—Elias and al-Khiḍr—meet each year in Mecca.’ Ibn ʿAbbās said: ‘We were informed that one shaves the other’s head and tells him to recite, “In the name of God,”’ followed by the preceding words. He added that Ibn ʿAbbās said the Messenger of God ﷺ stated: ‘No servant recites them each day without being protected until evening from burning, drowning, theft, and everything he dislikes; likewise when he recites them in the morning.’ Ibn al-Jawzī said that Aḥmad ibn ʿAmmār was abandoned according to al-Dāraquṭnī, and Mahdī ibn Hilāl was likewise. Ibn Ḥibbān said Mahdī ibn Hilāl related fabricated reports.

Through ʿUbayd ibn Isḥāq al-ʿAṭṭār, from Muḥammad ibn Maysar, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan, from his father, from his grandfather, from ʿAlī, it is reported that Gabriel, Michael, Raphael, and al-Khiḍr meet every Day of ʿArafa. Gabriel says, ‘What God wills; there is no power except through God.’ Michael responds, ‘What God wills; every blessing comes from God.’ Raphael responds, ‘What God wills; all good is in God’s hand.’ Al-Khiḍr responds, ‘What God wills; none averts evil except God.’ They then part and do not meet again until the same day of the next year. ʿUbayd ibn Isḥāq is abandoned in hadith.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad transmitted in the additions to his father’s Kitāb al-Zuhd, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād, that al-Khiḍr and Elias meet at Jerusalem throughout Ramadan, break their fast with celery, and attend the pilgrimage season each year. This report omits two or more successive links.

In the Fawāʾid of Abū ʿAlī Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Bāshānī, we transmitted from ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ibn Ḥabīb al-Firyābī, from Ṣāliḥ, from Asad ibn Saʿīd, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his forefathers, from ʿAlī, who said: ‘I was with the Prophet ﷺ when oils were mentioned before him. He said: “The merit of violet oil above all oils is like our merit, the Household, above all creation.”’ The Prophet ﷺ used to apply it as oil and take it through the nose. The rest is a long hadith mentioning leek, sweet basil, watercress, chicory, truffles, celery, meat, and fish. It includes the claims that truffles come from Paradise, their water heals the eye and cures poison, and that truffles and celery are the food of Elias and Elisha. They meet each year during the pilgrimage season and drink one draught of Zamzam water, which suffices them until the next year. God renews their youth once every one hundred years, and their food is truffles and celery. Ibn al-Jawzī said there was no doubt this hadith was fabricated and that its accused fabricator was ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ibn Ḥabīb; Ibn Ḥibbān said he used to fabricate hadith. Muqātil’s earlier claim that Elisha was al-Khiḍr has already appeared.

Ibn Shāhīn said that Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥarrānī related from Abū Ṭāhir Khayr ibn ʿArafa, from Hāniʾ ibn al-Mutawakkil, from Baqiyya, from al-Awzāʿī, from Makḥūl, who heard Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ say: ‘We accompanied the Messenger of God ﷺ on the expedition to Tabūk. When we reached the territory of Judhām, we had become thirsty. We saw signs of rain ahead, traveled one mile, and found a pool. After a third of the night had passed, a caller with a sorrowful voice cried: “O God, make me one of Muḥammad’s community, which receives mercy, forgiveness, answered prayer, and blessing.” The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Ḥudhayfa and Anas, enter this mountain pass and see whose voice this is.”

‘We entered and found a man dressed in garments whiter than snow. His face and beard were likewise white, and he stood two or three cubits taller than us. We greeted him and he returned our greeting, then said: “Welcome, you two are envoys of the Messenger.” We said yes and asked who he was. He replied: “I am the prophet Elias. I set out for Mecca and saw your army. A company of angels told me: Gabriel is at their front and Michael at their rear; this is your brother, the Messenger of God ﷺ, so greet and meet him. Return and convey my greeting of peace. Tell him that the only thing preventing me from entering your army is my fear that the camels would be startled and the Muslims frightened by my height, for my form is unlike yours. Tell him ﷺ to come to me.”

‘Ḥudhayfa and Anas said: “We shook his hand. He asked Anas, ‘Servant of the Messenger of God, who is this?’ Anas said, ‘Ḥudhayfa, keeper of the Messenger of God’s secret.’ He welcomed him and said, ‘By God, he is better known in heaven than on earth; the inhabitants of heaven call him the keeper of the Messenger of God’s secret.’ Ḥudhayfa asked whether he met the angels. Elias replied, ‘Not a day passes without my meeting them; they greet me and I greet them.’”

‘We went to the Prophet ﷺ, and he came with us to the pass. Elias’s face and clothing shone like the sun. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Stay where you are,” and we advanced about fifty cubits. He embraced Elias at length and they sat. We saw things resembling huge white birds surround them, spread their wings, and screen them from us. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ called to us: “Ḥudhayfa and Anas, come forward.” Before them was a green table more beautiful than anything I had ever seen. Its green overwhelmed our whiteness, so that our faces and clothes appeared green. Upon it were cheese, dates, pomegranates, bananas, grapes, fresh dates, and herbs other than leek. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Eat in the name of God.” We asked: “Messenger of God, is this food from the world?” He answered no.’

‘Elias told us: “This is my provision. I receive one meal every forty days and nights. These forty days have now ended. It is something to which God says ‘Be,’ and it is.” We asked where he had come from. He said: “From beyond Byzantium. I was with an army of angels and an army of Muslim jinn fighting a nation of unbelievers.” The place was four months away; he had left them ten days earlier and was heading to Mecca. He drank one draught there each year, which quenched and sustained him until the next pilgrimage season. The places he frequented most were Syria, Jerusalem, the west, and Yemen, and there was no mosque belonging to Muḥammad, small or great, that he did not enter.

‘We asked when he had last seen al-Khiḍr. He said: “A year ago. He and I met at the pilgrimage season, as I meet him each season. He told me, ‘You will meet Muḥammad, so convey my greeting of peace to him.’” Elias embraced him and wept, then embraced us; he wept and we wept. We watched him rise into the sky as though he were a lifted burden. We said: “Messenger of God, we have seen a wonder in his ascent.” He said: “He is carried between an angel’s wings until the angel delivers him wherever he wishes.”’

Ibn al-Jawzī said: ‘Perhaps Baqiyya heard this from a liar and concealed him by ambiguously attributing it to al-Awzāʿī. Nor is it known who Khayr ibn ʿArafa was.’ I say: he was a well-known Egyptian hadith scholar, whose grandfather was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kāmil and whose teknonym was Abū Ṭāhir. Abū Ṭālib al-Ḥāfiẓ, the shaykh of al-Dāraquṭnī, and others related from him. He died in 283. Someone other than Baqiyya transmitted it from al-Awzāʿī in a different form.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā said that Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿīd al-Jawharī related from Yazīd ibn Yazīd al-Mawṣilī al-Taymī, their client, from Abū Isḥāq al-Jurashī, from al-Awzāʿī, from Makḥūl, from Anas: ‘We went on campaign with the Messenger of God ﷺ. When we reached Fajj al-Nāqa near al-Ḥijr, we heard a voice saying, “O God, make me one of Muḥammad’s community, which receives mercy, forgiveness, repentance, and answered prayer.” The Messenger of God ﷺ told me: “Anas, find out whose voice that is.” I entered the mountain and found a white-haired, white-bearded man in white clothing, more than three hundred cubits tall. When he saw me he asked whether I was the Messenger’s envoy. I said yes. He said: “Return, convey my greeting of peace, and tell him that his brother Elias wishes to meet him.”

‘The Prophet ﷺ came, with me accompanying him. When we drew near, he advanced and I remained behind. They conversed at length. Something resembling a dining cloth descended upon them from heaven. They invited me, and I ate with them. It held truffles, pomegranates, and celery. After eating I rose and withdrew. A cloud came and carried Elias away, and I could see the whiteness of his clothes as it bore him toward Syria. I asked the Prophet ﷺ: “May my father and mother be your ransom, did this food we ate descend from heaven for you?” He said: “I asked Elias about it. He told me, ‘Gabriel brings me one meal every forty days and one draught of Zamzam water each year. At times I see him at the well holding the bucket and drinking; at times he gives me water.’”’

Ibn al-Jawzī said that neither Yazīd nor Isḥāq was known, and this version conflicts with the preceding one over Elias’s height. Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted by way of ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Dawrī, from Hishām ibn Khālid, from al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā al-Khushanī, from Ibn Abī Rawwād that al-Khiḍr and Elias fast at Jerusalem, perform Hajj each year, and drink one draught of Zamzam that suffices them until the same time the following year.

I then found in ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal’s additions to al-Zuhd: ‘I found in my father’s handwriting that Mahdī ibn Jaʿfar related from Ḍamra, from al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from Ibn Abī Rawwād, who said: “Elias and al-Khiḍr fast the month of Ramadan in Jerusalem and attend the pilgrimage season every year.”’ ʿAbd Allāh also related the same from al-Ḥasan ibn Rāfiʿ, from Ḍamra, from al-Sarī, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād. Ibn Jarīr said in his Tārīkh that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam al-Miṣrī related from Muḥammad ibn al-Mutawakkil, from Ḍamra ibn Rabīʿa, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shawdhab: ‘Al-Khiḍr descends from Persia and Elias from the Israelites. They meet each year during the pilgrimage season.’

Reports Concerning Al-Khiḍr’s Survival After the Prophet ﷺ and Those Who Related Seeing and Speaking With Him

Al-Fākihī said in Kitāb Makka that al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār related from Ḥamza ibn ʿUtba, from Muḥammad ibn ʿImrān, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī—al-Ṣādiq son of al-Bāqir. Jaʿfar said: ‘I was with my father in Mecca during the ten nights. He was standing in prayer at the Ḥijr when a white-haired, white-bearded man of thick limbs entered and sat beside him. My father shortened his prayer. The man asked him, “May God have mercy on you, tell me about the first creation of this House.” My father asked who he was. He said he came from the far west. My father replied: “When God rebuked the angels after they said, ‘Will You place in it one who causes corruption?’ [Qur’an 2:30], they circled His Throne seeking pardon. He accepted their excuse and was pleased with them, then said, ‘Make for Me a house upon earth. Any of My servants with whom I am angry may circle it, and I shall be pleased with him as I was pleased with you.’” The man said: “Indeed, may God have mercy on you. No one of your age remains more learned than you,” and departed. My father told me to catch him and bring him back. I followed him until the Ṣafā gate, where he vanished as though he had never existed. When I told my father, he said: “Do you know who that was? That was al-Khiḍr.”’

Al-Zubayr also gave this report with the same chain in Kitāb al-Nasab. In that version the man had white hair and beard, massive bones, broad shoulders and chest, and wore two coarse garments like a pilgrim in consecration. He sat beside Abū Jaʿfar, who understood that he wanted the prayer shortened, concluded it, and turned toward him. Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted through Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīra, from his father, from his grandfather that the attendants of the mosque told al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik that al-Khiḍr prayed there every night.

Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Jabalī said in al-Dībāj that ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Anṭākī related from ʿAlī ibn al-Haytham al-Maṣṣīṣī, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Baḥr, from Sallām al-Ṭawīl, from Dāwūd ibn ʿAwn al-Ṭafāwī, from a man who had guarded the frontier at Jerusalem and Ashkelon. The man said: ‘While traveling through the Jordan Valley, I saw a man praying at its side beneath a cloud that shaded him from the sun. It occurred to me that he was the prophet Elias. I greeted him; he finished his prayer and returned the greeting. When I repeatedly asked who he was, he said, “I am the prophet Elias.” I trembled so violently that I feared losing my mind and asked him to pray for its removal so I could understand him. He prayed using eight invocations: “O Most Kind, O Most Merciful, O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting, O Most Compassionate, O Bestower, O Hayāshar, O Ahyā,” and the feeling left me.

‘I asked to whom he had been sent. He said the people of Baalbek. I asked whether revelation still came to him; he replied that it had not since Muḥammad, Seal of the Prophets, was sent. He said that four prophets remained alive: he and al-Khiḍr on earth, and Enoch and Jesus in heaven. He met al-Khiḍr every year at ʿArafāt, and each cut the other’s hair. There were sixty substitutes: fifty between al-ʿArīsh in Egypt and the Euphrates shore, two at al-Maṣṣīṣa, one at Antioch, and seven throughout the other cities. Through them rain was provided, victory granted over enemies, and God maintained the world’s order; when He wished to destroy the world, He would cause them all to die.’ Its chain contains unknown and abandoned transmitters.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim said in his Tafsīr that his father related from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Awsī, from ʿAlī ibn Abī ʿAlī al-Hāshimī, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, from his father: when the Prophet ﷺ died and words of consolation came, the Household heard a visitor’s voice without seeing him. He said: ‘Peace, God’s mercy, and His blessings be upon you, Household. Every soul shall taste death, and you will receive your recompense in full only on the Day of Resurrection [Qur’an 3:185]. In God is consolation for every calamity, a successor to every lost one, and recovery of everything missed. Trust God and place your hope in Him, for the truly afflicted is one denied the reward.’ Jaʿfar said that his father informed him that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib asked: ‘Do you know who that was? It was al-Khiḍr.’

Muḥammad ibn Manṣūr al-Jazzār transmitted it from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maymūn al-Qaddāḥ, both from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, who heard his father say: ‘When the Messenger of God ﷺ died, a visitor’s words of consolation came. They heard his voice but did not see him: “Peace and God’s mercy be upon you, Household. In God is consolation for every calamity, a successor to every lost one, and recovery of everything missed. Trust God and place your hope in Him, for the one truly deprived is denied the reward.” ʿAlī asked: “Do you know who that was? It was al-Khiḍr.”’

Ibn al-Jawzī said that Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ corroborated Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, but Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ was weak. I say: al-Wāqidī, who was a liar, also related it. Ibn al-Jawzī said that Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmar related it from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar and that Ibn Abī ʿUmar was unknown. I say: that unqualified judgment is weak. Ibn Abī ʿUmar is far too famous to be described thus: he was a trustworthy master with a well-known, transmitted Musnad, and was a shaykh of Muslim and other leading scholars.

I received this hadith from our shaykh, the leading memorizer of the age, Abū al-Faḍl ibn al-Ḥusayn ﵀, who received it from Abū Muḥammad ibn al-Qayyim, from Abū al-Ḥasan ibn al-Bukhārī, from Muḥammad ibn Muʿammar, from Saʿīd ibn Abī al-Rajāʾ, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Nuʿmān, from Abū Bakr ibn al-Muqriʾ, from Isḥāq ibn Aḥmad al-Khuzāʿī, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿUmar al-ʿAdanī, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad. He said that his father, Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad al-Ṣādiq, related from his father, from his grandfather, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that a group of Quraysh entered upon them. ʿAlī asked: ‘Shall I tell you about Abū al-Qāsim?’ They said yes, and he related at length the death of the Prophet ﷺ.

At its end, Gabriel said: ‘Aḥmad, peace be upon you. This is the last time I shall tread the earth. You alone were my purpose in the world.’ When the Messenger of God ﷺ died and the consolation came, they heard a visitor’s voice without seeing him: ‘Peace and God’s mercy be upon you, Household. In God is consolation for every calamity, a successor to every lost one, and recovery of everyone missed. Trust God and place your hope in Him, for the deprived is one denied reward, and the afflicted is one denied reward. Peace be upon you.’ ʿAlī asked whether they knew who it was and said it was al-Khiḍr.

This Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar was the brother of Mūsā al-Kāẓim. He related from his father and others, and Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir and others related from him. He proclaimed his own claim in Medina and Mecca; in the year 200 the people pledged allegiance to him as caliph and he led the pilgrimage. Al-Muʿtaṣim performed Hajj, captured him, and carried him to his brother al-Maʾmūn in Khurasan. He died at Gurgān in 203. Al-Khaṭīb stated in his biography that after his capture he mounted the pulpit and said: ‘People, I related to you hadiths that I forged.’ The people tore up the books they had heard from him. He lived seventy years. Al-Bukhārī said his brother Isḥāq was more trustworthy. Al-Ḥākim transmitted from him a hadith that al-Dhahabī called manifestly objectionable in its mention of Solomon son of David ﵉.

Al-Bayhaqī said in al-Dalāʾil that Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥāfiẓ related from Abū Jaʿfar al-Baghdādī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣanʿānī, from Abū al-Walīd al-Makhzūmī, from Anas ibn ʿIyāḍ, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh: ‘When the Messenger of God ﷺ died, the angels consoled them. They heard the voice but saw no one: “Peace, God’s mercy, and His blessings be upon you. In God is consolation for every calamity and a successor to everyone missed. Trust God and place your hope in Him, for the deprived is only one denied the reward. Peace, God’s mercy, and His blessings be upon you.”’

Al-Bayhaqī also transmitted from Abū Saʿīd Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr al-Aḥmasī, from al-Ḥasan ibn Ḥumayd ibn al-Rabīʿ al-Lakhmī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ziyād, from Sayyār ibn Abī Ḥātim, from ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Sulaymān al-Ḥārithī, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī: before the death of the Messenger of God ﷺ, Gabriel descended to him. He related the death account at length, including that after it a visitor came whose voice they heard but whose person they did not see. He greeted them with peace, God’s mercy, and His blessings, and offered consolation in words like those above.

Sayf ibn ʿUmar al-Tamīmī transmitted in his Kitāb al-Ridda from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Ibn ʿUmar: when the Messenger of God ﷺ died, Abū Bakr came and entered. On seeing him covered, he said, ‘Indeed we belong to God, and to Him we return,’ then prayed over him. The Household raised a wail that the people at the prayer ground heard. When they quieted, they heard a strong, resonant man at the door greeting the Household and saying: ‘Every soul shall taste death, and you will receive your recompense in full only on the Day of Resurrection [Qur’an 3:185]. Truly, in God is a successor to everyone, deliverance from every fear. Hope in God and trust Him, for the afflicted is one denied the reward.’ They listened and ceased weeping, then looked out and saw no one. When they resumed, another caller said: ‘Household, remember and praise God in every condition, and you will be among the sincere. In God is consolation for every calamity and compensation for every loss. Trust God and obey Him, for the afflicted is one denied reward.’ Abū Bakr said: ‘Al-Khiḍr and Elias have attended the death of the Messenger of God ﷺ.’ There is criticism of the chain, and Sayf’s shaykh is unknown.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā said that Kāmil ibn Ṭalḥa related from ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbd al-Ṣamad, from Anas ibn Mālik: ‘When the Messenger of God ﷺ died, his Companions gathered around him, weeping. A hairy, broad-shouldered man wearing a waist-wrapper and cloak entered, stepping past the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ until he grasped the two doorposts of the house. He wept, then turned to the Companions and said: “In God is consolation for every calamity, compensation for everything missed, and a successor to everyone lost. Turn to God and consider His regard for you during affliction, for the afflicted is only one who does not obtain the reward.” He left, and Abū Bakr said: “Bring me the man.” They looked right and left but saw no one. Abū Bakr said: “Perhaps this was al-Khiḍr, the brother of our Prophet, who came to console us over him ﷺ.”’

Al-Bukhārī and al-ʿUqaylī weakened ʿAbbād. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it in al-Awsaṭ from Mūsā ibn Abī Hārūn, from Kāmil, and said that ʿAbbād alone related it from Anas.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār said in Kitāb al-Nasab that Ḥamza ibn ʿUtba al-Lahabī related from Muḥammad ibn ʿImrān, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad al-Ṣādiq. Jaʿfar said: ‘I was with my father Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī in Mecca during the ten nights, a day or two before the day of Tarwiya. My father was standing in prayer at the Ḥijr and I sat behind him. A white-haired, white-bearded man of massive bones, broad shoulders and chest, wearing two coarse garments like a pilgrim in consecration, came and sat beside him. My father knew he wished him to shorten the prayer, so he concluded it and turned to him. The man said: “Abū Jaʿfar, tell me how the creation of this House began.” My father asked who he was. He said he was a man from Syria.

‘Abū Jaʿfar said: “The beginning of this House was when God ﵎ said to the angels, ‘I am placing a vicegerent upon the earth.’ They replied, ‘Will You place in it one who causes corruption?’ [Qur’an 2:30]. God became angry with them, so they sought refuge at the Throne and circled it seven times, seeking their Lord’s pleasure. He was pleased with them and said: ‘Build for Me a house upon earth. Any descendant of Adam with whom I am angry may seek refuge there and circle it as you circled My Throne, and I shall be pleased with them.’ They built this House.” The man then asked: “Abū Jaʿfar, what enters this corner?”’ The rest of the story follows.

Jaʿfar said: ‘The man rose and left. My father instructed me to bring him back. I followed, supposing the crowd stood between us. He headed toward al-Ṣafā; I searched al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa but did not find him. When I told my father, he said: “You were never going to find him; that was al-Khiḍr.”’

Ibn Shāhīn said in Kitāb al-Janāʾiz that Ibn Abī Dāwūd related from Aḥmad ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Sarrāj, from Ibn Wahb, from an unnamed transmitter, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir: while ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was conducting a funeral prayer, a caller behind him cried, ‘Do not begin the prayer before us; may God have mercy on you.’ ʿUmar waited until the man joined the row and pronounced the takbīr. The man prayed: ‘If You punish him, he disobeyed You; if You forgive him, he is in need of Your mercy.’

After the burial, the man leveled soil over the grave and said: ‘Glad tidings to you, occupant of the grave, if you were not an inspector, traitor, treasurer, scribe, or policeman.’ ʿUmar told his companions to seize the man and ask him about his prayer and words. The man turned away, leaving a footprint one cubit long. ʿUmar said: ‘By God, this is al-Khiḍr, about whom the Prophet ﷺ told us.’ Ibn al-Jawzī said there is an unknown transmitter in the chain and a break between Ibn al-Munkadir and ʿUmar.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā said that his father related from ʿAlī ibn Shaqīq, from Ibn al-Mubārak, from ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir: while a man walked selling something and swearing oaths, an old man stopped him and said, ‘Sell, but do not swear.’ When the seller again swore, the old man repeated himself. The seller told him to mind his own business. The old man said: ‘This is my business. Prefer truth when it harms you to falsehood when it benefits you. Speak, but when your knowledge ends, be silent; suspect a liar when he tells you what another person said.’ The seller asked him to write these words. The old man replied, ‘Whatever is decreed will be,’ then disappeared. They believed him to have been al-Khiḍr. Ibn al-Jawzī said this was apparently the report’s original form.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Sammāk transmitted in his Fawāʾid from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ṭālib, from ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd Allāh that Ibn ʿUmar was sitting while a man repeatedly swore oaths over goods he wished to sell. A passerby told him: ‘Fear God and do not swear falsely by Him. Adhere to truth when it harms you, beware of falsehood when it benefits you, and do not add to another person’s report.’ Ibn ʿUmar sent someone after the passerby to ask him to write the words. He replied, ‘Whatever is decreed will be,’ then vanished. Ibn ʿUmar said: ‘That was al-Khiḍr.’ Ibn al-Jawzī said that ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim was weak and had a poor memory, and perhaps intended to say ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir but instead said Ibn ʿUmar. Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Muṣʿab, a fabricator, transmitted it from a group of unknown men, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar.

I say: I found another, sound route from Ibn ʿUmar. Al-Bayhaqī said in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa that Abū Zakariyyā ibn Abī Isḥāq related from Aḥmad ibn Sulaymān al-Faqīh, from al-Ḥasan ibn Mukram, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bakr al-Sahmī, from al-Ḥajjāj ibn Furāfiṣa: two men were trading in the presence of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, and one swore many oaths. A man overheard, stood over them, and said: ‘Servant of God, fear God and do not swear frequently. Your oath will neither increase your provision nor will abstaining decrease it.’ The seller told him to move on. He replied three times that it concerned him. Before leaving he said: ‘Know that part of faith is to prefer truth where it harms you to falsehood where it benefits you, and let your words not exceed your deeds.’

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar sent someone after him to write down the words. The man replied, ‘Servant of God, write these words for me; may God have mercy on you.’ The passerby said, ‘Whatever God decrees will be,’ and repeated the words until the messenger memorized them. He then walked away, placed one foot in the mosque, and the observer could no longer tell whether earth or sky was beneath him. They seemed to believe he was al-Khiḍr or Elias.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā said that Yaʿqūb ibn Yūsuf related from Mālik ibn Ismāʿīl, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Aswad, from Maḥfūẓ ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from a shaykh of Hadramawt, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: ‘While I circled the House, I saw a man clinging to its coverings and saying, “O You whom nothing distracts from hearing, O You whom petitioners do not overwhelm, O You who does not weary of those who persist: let me taste the coolness of Your pardon and the sweetness of Your mercy.” I asked him to repeat his prayer. He asked whether I had heard it. When I said yes, he told me to recite it after every prayer, and said: “By Him in whose hand is al-Khiḍr’s soul, if your sins equaled the stars of heaven and the pebbles of earth, God would forgive you faster than the blink of an eye.”’ Al-Dīnawarī transmitted it by this route in al-Mujālasa.

Aḥmad ibn Ḥarb al-Naysābūrī related a similar report from Muḥammad ibn Muʿādh al-Harawī, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muḥarrar, from Yazīd ibn al-Aṣamm, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. In this version the man said: ‘By Him in whose hand is al-Khiḍr’s soul,’ and that al-Khiḍr would say these words after the prescribed prayer; anyone who said them then would have his sins forgiven, even if they equaled the sands of ʿĀlij, the raindrops, and the leaves of trees. Muḥammad ibn Muʿādh al-Harawī also related it from Abū ʿUbayd Allāh al-Makhzūmī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Walīd, from Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, similarly.

Sayf related in al-Futūḥ that a group accompanying Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ saw Abū Miḥjan fighting. He related Abū Miḥjan’s lengthy story and said that, not recognizing the fighter, they declared: ‘It can only be al-Khiḍr.’ This implies that they were certain al-Khiḍr existed then.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Baṭṭa al-ʿUkbarī al-Ḥanbalī said that Shuʿayb ibn Aḥmad related from Aḥmad ibn Abī al-ʿAwwām, from his father, from Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd al-Wāsiṭī, from Abīn ibn Sufyān, from Ghālib ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿUqaylī, from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: a Sunni and Ghaylān the Qadarite disagreed about predestination and agreed to let the first man who appeared from a specified direction judge between them. A Bedouin came with his cloak folded upon his shoulder. They accepted him as judge; he spread his cloak, sat on it, seated them before him, and ruled against Ghaylān. Al-Ḥasan said: ‘That was al-Khiḍr.’ Its chain contains Abīn ibn Sufyān, who was abandoned in hadith.

Ḥammād ibn ʿUmar al-Naṣībī, himself one of the abandoned transmitters, related from al-Sarī ibn Khālid, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from his grandfather ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn: a client of theirs sailed and was shipwrecked. As he walked along the shore he saw a man by the sea and a table descend from heaven before him. The man ate, and it was lifted. The survivor asked: ‘By the One who enabled you to receive what I saw, which servant of God are you?’ He replied: ‘The al-Khiḍr of whom you have heard.’ Asked what had brought him the food and drink, he said: ‘The mighty names of God.’

Aḥmad transmitted in al-Zuhd from Ḥammād ibn Usāma, from Misʿar, from Maʿn ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba: during the upheaval of Ibn al-Zubayr, a troubled man in an Egyptian garden sat bent over, scratching the earth. He looked up and saw a young man with a spade standing before him. He seemed to look down on the youth, who asked why he was troubled. The man said it was nothing. The youth replied: ‘If it is the world, this world is a present commodity from which righteous and wicked eat. The Hereafter is an appointed term that shall come true, in which an omnipotent King will judge.’ He described it as having distinct joints like the joints of meat: whoever missed one missed the truth.

The man admired his words and explained that his concern was for the Muslims. The youth said: ‘God will save you because of your compassion for the Muslims. Who has ever asked God without receiving, called upon Him without an answer, relied upon Him without His sufficing him, or trusted Him without His deliverance?’ The man began saying: ‘O God, keep me safe, and keep others safe from me.’ The turmoil cleared, and he was untouched. Misʿar said they believed the youth was al-Khiḍr. Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it in ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s biography in al-Ḥilya by way of Abū Usāma—Ḥammād ibn Usāma—and added that Ibn ʿUyayna related it from Abū Misʿar.

After Muslim’s narration of Abū Saʿīd’s hadith about the man whom the Antichrist kills, Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn Sufyān, Muslim’s transmitter, said that this man was said to be al-Khiḍr. ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, from Abū Saʿīd the full Antichrist account, including the man he kills. At its end Maʿmar said: ‘I was informed that a copper plate is placed upon his throat, and I was informed that he is al-Khiḍr.’ Al-Nawawī attributed this to Maʿmar’s Musnad in a way suggesting it had a chain there, although it is only Maʿmar’s statement.

Abū Nuʿaym transmitted in al-Ḥilya through a chain ending with Aḥmad ibn Ḥumayd, who said that Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna related: ‘While I circled the House, I saw a man standing above the crowd with a handsome gray beard. We said to one another that he looked like a scholar and followed him. After completing his circumambulation, he went to Abraham’s Station and prayed two cycles.’

‘After concluding, the man faced the qibla and made supplications, then turned to us and asked: “Do you know what your Lord says?” We asked what He said. He replied: “Your Lord says, ‘I am the King; I invite you to become kings.’” He again faced the qibla, prayed, turned to us, and asked the same. He said: “Your Lord says, ‘I am the Living who never dies; I invite you to become living ones who never die.’” A third time he prayed and asked. He said: “Your Lord says, ‘I am the One whose wish comes into being whenever I will something; I invite you to attain a state in which whatever you wish will come to you.’”’ Ibn ʿUyayna said the man left and they did not see him again. When he told Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Thawrī said: ‘How closely he resembles al-Khiḍr or one of these substitutes.’ Muḥriz ibn Abī Jadhʿa corroborated Sufyān, as did Ziyād ibn Abī al-Aṣbagh; Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Azhar also related a similar version from al-ʿAbbās ibn Yazīd, from Sufyān.

Abū Saʿīd transmitted in Sharaf al-Muṣṭafā, by way of Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Barza, from Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt, from Maysara ibn Saʿīd, from his father: al-Ḥasan sat in a gathering surrounded by people when a man with greenish eyes approached. Al-Ḥasan asked whether his mother had borne him that way or whether it was an affliction. The man asked: ‘Do you not recognize me, Abū Saʿīd?’ He identified himself, and everyone present knew him. Al-Ḥasan asked his story.

The man said: ‘I put all my property aboard a ship bound for China. A gale wrecked it, and I reached a shore upon a plank. For about four months I wandered, eating whatever trees and plants I found and drinking spring water. I resolved to move straight ahead until I either perished or reached habitation. I saw what looked like a silver palace. I pushed open its door and found galleries, each recess holding a pearl casket with visible locks and keys. I opened some, and a sweet fragrance emerged. Within were men wrapped in various kinds of silk, dead but appearing alive. I closed the casket, left, and shut the palace door.

‘Two horsemen of incomparable beauty then came upon dappled horses with white markings. When I told them my story, they directed me to a tree ahead with a meadow beneath it, where a handsome old man prayed upon a raised platform. They said he would guide me to the road. I found him, greeted him, and related everything. He was alarmed by the palace, but relaxed when I said I had closed the caskets and doors. As I sat, one cloud after another passed and greeted him, “Peace be upon you, friend of God.” He asked each its destination. Finally a cloud bound for Basra came. He told it to descend, and it settled before him. He commanded: “Carry this man and return him safely to his home.”

‘Once upon the cloud, I implored him by the One who had honored him to identify the palace, the two horsemen, and himself. He said: “God honored those who drowned as martyrs of the sea and appointed angels to collect them from the water and place them in those caskets, wrapped in silk shrouds. The two horsemen are angels who bring them God’s greeting morning and evening. I am al-Khiḍr, and I have asked my Lord to resurrect me with the community of your Prophet.” When the cloud carried me, terror overwhelmed me and left me as you see.’ Al-Ḥasan said: ‘You have witnessed something tremendous.’

Al-Ṭabarānī said in Kitāb al-Duʿāʾ that Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad al-Ḥannāʾī related from al-Muʿallā ibn Ḥarmī, from Muḥammad ibn al-Muhājir al-Baṣrī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Tawʾam al-Raqāshī: Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik frightened a man and sought to kill him. The man fled. Sulaymān’s agents repeatedly searched his house without finding him, and wherever the man went he was told that he had just been sought there. When this persisted, he resolved to go somewhere outside Sulaymān’s authority. The narrator then related a long story: in a desert without tree or water, the fugitive saw a man praying. He was afraid but, having neither mount nor beast, approached. The man bowed and prostrated, then turned and said: ‘Perhaps this tyrant has frightened you.’ The fugitive said yes. The man asked: ‘What prevents you from using the seven?’

The fugitive asked what ‘the seven’ were. The man said: ‘Recite: Glory be to the One besides whom there is no god; glory be to the Beginningless One who has no beginning; glory be to the Everlasting One who has no end; glory be to the One who is every day upon some affair; glory be to the One who gives life and causes death; glory be to the One who created what we see and what we do not see; glory be to the One who knows everything without being taught.’ The fugitive recited and memorized them, then turned and no longer saw the man. God cast security into his heart, and he retraced his route to his family.

He decided to go to Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik’s door. It was a day of public audience, and he entered. As soon as Sulaymān saw him, he sat upright, beckoned him ever closer, and seated him beside himself upon the couch. Sulaymān said: ‘You have bewitched me, and are a sorcerer besides, according to what I heard about you.’ The man denied knowing or using sorcery. Sulaymān said: ‘How, then? I thought my rule would not be complete unless I killed you, yet on seeing you I could not stop until I summoned and seated you beside me.’ He demanded the truth, and the man told his story. Sulaymān said: ‘By God, besides whom there is no god, al-Khiḍr taught you those words.’ He ordered a safe-conduct written for the man, a generous gift given him, and transport provided to his family.

In Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa’s biography in al-Ḥilya, Abū Nuʿaym transmitted from Tārīkh al-Sarrāj, by way of Muḥammad ibn Dhakwān, from Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa: ‘I was standing with Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and held a position of favor with him when a handsome-looking man came and greeted us. He said: “Rajāʾ, you have been tested by this man, and proximity to him brings deviation. Adhere to what is right and aid the weak. Know that one who holds a position with the ruler and raises the need of a weak person who cannot raise it himself will meet God on the Day of Resurrection with his feet made firm for the reckoning. One who attends to the need of his Muslim brother will have God attend to his need. Know, Rajāʾ, that one of the deeds most beloved to God is joy you bring to a Muslim.”’ The man then disappeared, and Rajāʾ believed him to have been al-Khiḍr ﵇.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār said in al-Muwaffaqiyyāt that al-Sarī ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anṣārī, a descendant of al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ṣimma, related from Muṣʿab ibn Thābit ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, who prayed one thousand cycles each day and night and fasted perpetually. Muṣʿab said: ‘I spent a night in the mosque. After the people left, a man came to the Prophet ﷺ, greeted him, leaned against the wall, and said: “O God, You know that I ended yesterday fasting without eating, and that I have remained fasting today and again reached evening without eating. O God, this evening I desire tharīd, so feed me from Yourself.”

‘I saw a servant enter through an opening in the minaret. His form was unlike that of human beings, and he carried a bowl. He placed it before the man, who began eating, then tossed a pebble at me and said: “Come.” I approached, thinking it came from Paradise and wishing to taste it. I ate one morsel; it resembled no food of this world. I then became shy and returned to my place. When the man finished, the servant took the bowl and withdrew by the same route. The man rose to leave, and I followed to identify him. He became indistinguishable, and I did not know which path he took. I thought him to be al-Khiḍr.’

Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī said in the aforementioned treatise that Aḥmad ibn Mulāʿib related from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Saʿīdī, from Abū Jaʿfar al-Kūfī, from Abū ʿUmar al-Naṣībī. Abū ʿUmar went searching in Syria for Maslama ibn Maṣqala, who was said to be one of the substitutes. He met him in the Jordan Valley. Maslama said: ‘Shall I tell you something I saw in this valley today? I entered it and found an old man praying toward a tree. It occurred to me that he was the prophet Elias. I drew near and greeted him. He completed the prayer and returned my greeting. When I asked who he was, he said: “I am the prophet Elias.”’

Maslama continued: ‘I trembled so violently that I fell upon my back. Elias approached and placed his hand before me; I felt its coolness between my shoulders. I asked him to pray that the feeling leave me so I could understand his words. He invoked God by eight names, five Arabic and three Syriac: “O One, O Unique, O Everlasting Refuge, O Singular, O Odd,” followed by three I did not recognize. He took my hand and seated me, and the feeling left.

‘I asked whether he had seen what that man—Marwān ibn Muḥammad, then besieging the people of Homs—was doing. Elias asked why I concerned myself with an insolent tyrant against God. I said I had passed by him. Elias turned away. I explained that although I had passed the two sides, I favored neither, and that I sought God’s forgiveness and repented to Him. He faced me and said: “You have done well. Say that, and do not repeat it.”
